topics.title: Tenali Raman-style wit: reading a clever tale

learn.hook: What wins in a king's court when there is no sword in your hand? A sharp mind and a quick, kind reply!
points: The lesson 'The Wit that Won Hearts' is about how clever, good-humoured thinking can win people over.
Tenali Raman (Tenali Ramakrishna) was a poet in the court of King Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire in the 16th century. Folk tales about his clever answers are told all over India.
Wit is the ability to think quickly and say something clever and amusing. A witty person solves a problem with words and ideas, not with force.
Most wit tales follow a pattern: a tricky challenge, a clever plan or reply, and a surprising ending that makes people laugh and learn.
Wit wins hearts when it is kind: it makes a point and makes people smile without hurting anyone.

example.q: Read: A proud merchant told the court, "I can sell anything, even air!" Tenali handed him an empty jar. "Then sell me this jar of fresh Vijayanagara breeze for one gold coin." The merchant peeped in and said, "But it is empty!" "Exactly," said Tenali, "and so was your boast." The whole court laughed, even the merchant. Think it through: what made Tenali's reply witty?
steps: The merchant made a big boast: he could sell anything, even air.
Tenali turned the boast into a test by offering a jar of 'air'.
When the merchant called the jar empty, Tenali said the boast was empty too.
The reply was quick and funny, and it made its point without being cruel, so even the merchant laughed.
example.answer: Tenali used the merchant's own words against him in a quick, funny way, showing that the boast had nothing behind it.

learn.reallife: When a friend teases you and you answer with a friendly comeback that makes everyone laugh, including your friend, that is wit in action.

quiz.q: Read: 'A proud merchant told the court, "I can sell anything, even air!"' Tenali later called this a boast. What does 'boast' mean?
quiz.explain: A boast is talking proudly about what you can do or have. The merchant proudly claimed he could sell anything.
steps: The merchant proudly claimed he could sell anything, even air.
A boast is a proud claim about oneself, often bigger than the truth.
Answer: A proud claim about oneself
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'boast' with the similar-looking word 'boat'

quiz.q: Read: 'The merchant peeped in and said, "But it is empty!" "Exactly," said Tenali, "and so was your boast."' What does Tenali mean?
options: The merchant should buy a new jar
The jar was full of perfume
The merchant's claim had nothing real behind it
Tenali wanted the gold coin badly
quiz.explain: Tenali compares the empty jar to the empty boast: the merchant could not really sell 'anything'.
steps: The jar was empty, and Tenali says 'so was your boast'.
He means the merchant's claim was empty too — nothing real behind it.
Answer: The merchant's claim had nothing real behind it
quiz.mistake: Takes the words literally and misses the comparison

quiz.q: Which phrase is closest in meaning to 'witty'?
quiz.explain: A witty person says clever things that also make people smile.
steps: 'Witty' describes someone who says clever things that also amuse people.
So it means clever and amusing.
Answer: Clever and amusing
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'witty' just means careful or quiet thinking

quiz.q: Tenali Raman's tales are set in the court of which king?
quiz.explain: Tenali Raman was a poet in the court of Krishnadevaraya of the Vijayanagara Empire.
steps: Tenali Raman was a poet in the court of the Vijayanagara Empire.
Its king was Krishnadevaraya (Akbar's court had Birbal).
Answer: Krishnadevaraya
quiz.mistake: Mixes up Tenali Raman with Birbal, who is linked with Akbar

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of kind wit?
options: Making fun of a classmate's looks
A clever joke that makes everyone, even its target, laugh
Shouting louder than others in an argument
Copying someone's joke and claiming it as yours
quiz.explain: Kind wit makes a point and makes people laugh without hurting anyone.
steps: Kind wit makes a clever point without hurting anyone.
A joke that makes everyone, even its target, laugh fits; mocking looks or stealing jokes does not.
Answer: A clever joke that makes everyone, even its target, laugh
quiz.mistake: Thinks any joke at someone's cost counts as wit

quiz.q: Which word is the opposite of 'foolish'?
quiz.explain: Foolish means lacking good sense; wise means having good sense. The other words are close to 'foolish', not opposite.
steps: Foolish means lacking good sense.
Its opposite is wise; silly, careless and clumsy are close in meaning to foolish.
Answer: Wise
quiz.mistake: Picks a word with a similar meaning instead of the opposite

quiz.q: In a wit tale, what usually happens right after the hero hears the challenge?
options: The hero thinks of a clever plan
quiz.explain: The pattern is challenge, then clever plan, then the twist and the laugh at the end.
steps: The pattern of a wit tale: challenge → clever plan → twist → laugh.
So right after the challenge, the hero thinks of a clever plan.
Answer: The hero thinks of a clever plan
quiz.mistake: Jumps to the ending and forgets the planning step

quiz.q: Read: The king sighed, "My cook burnt the rice again. What shall I do, Raman?" Raman bowed. "Make him eat it, Your Majesty. He will never burn it again!" Why is Raman's answer funny?
options: It is rude to the king
It is a very long speech
It is an unexpected but clever solution
quiz.explain: The answer is surprising, yet it makes sense: a cook who has to eat burnt rice will be careful next time.
steps: Making the cook eat the burnt rice is surprising.
Yet it makes sense — he will be careful next time — so it is an unexpected but clever solution.
Answer: It is an unexpected but clever solution
quiz.mistake: Does not see that humour often comes from a surprising but sensible idea

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: What is 'wit'? How is a witty reply different from just being rude?
teach.praise: Chirp! Wit is quick, clever and funny, and it stays kind. Tenali would be proud of you!
teach.nudge: Is wit only about being clever? What should a witty reply do to the people listening, and should it hurt them?

revise.summary: 'The Wit that Won Hearts' shows how clever, good-humoured thinking can win people over, like Tenali Raman in King Krishnadevaraya's court. Kind wit solves problems with words, not force, and hurts no one.
focus: Explain what makes a reply witty in a short tale.
Know the pattern of a wit tale: challenge, clever plan or reply, surprising ending.
Recall that Tenali Raman was a poet in Krishnadevaraya's court (Vijayanagara Empire).
remember: Wit is the ability to think quickly and say something clever and amusing.
Wit tale pattern: a tricky challenge, a clever plan or reply, and a surprising ending.
Wit wins hearts when it is kind: it makes a point and makes people smile without hurting anyone.
traps: Don't mix up Tenali Raman (Krishnadevaraya) with Birbal (Akbar).
A joke that hurts someone is not kind wit.
Don't take a witty reply literally; look for the comparison, like the empty jar and the empty boast.

topics.title: Humour: idioms and funny expressions

learn.hook: If your friend says she is 'pulling your leg', should you check your leg? No! Welcome to the funny world of idioms.
points: Humour is the quality that makes something funny. 'Humour' is the British and Indian spelling; 'humor' is American. The adjective is 'humorous' in both, with no 'u' after the first 'o'.
Humour often comes from surprise, exaggeration (saying something is much bigger than it is) and funny misunderstandings.
An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words. 'Pulling my leg' means teasing me, not tugging my leg.

Useful humour idioms: crack a joke (tell a joke), in stitches (laughing a lot), keep a straight face (not laugh), tickled pink (very pleased), have the last laugh (win in the end after being doubted).

example.q: Think it through: Priya told Arjun, "Exams are cancelled forever!" Arjun's face lit up. Priya grinned, "I'm just pulling your leg!" What does Priya mean?
steps: Look at the idiom: 'pulling your leg'.
Nobody's leg is actually being pulled, so it is not literal.
Priya grinned after saying something too good to be true.
So the idiom means she was teasing or joking.
example.answer: Priya was joking; exams are not really cancelled.

learn.reallife: Comedy shows, cartoons and the jokes your grandparents tell at family dinners are full of exaggeration and idioms.

games.title: Idiom and meaning

items.text: The clown was so funny that the audience was in ___.
Dadaji tried to keep a ___ face while telling the joke.
Don't believe him, he is just pulling your ___.
Rohan loves to ___ jokes at the dinner table.

quiz.q: What does the idiom 'to pull someone's leg' mean?
quiz.explain: It is an idiom, so it is not about a real leg. It means joking with someone by telling them something untrue.
steps: 'Pull someone's leg' is an idiom, not about a real leg.
It means teasing someone playfully by saying something untrue.
Answer: To tease someone playfully
quiz.mistake: Takes the idiom literally

quiz.q: 'The comedian had us in stitches.' This means the audience was ___.
quiz.explain: 'In stitches' means laughing so much that your sides hurt.
steps: 'In stitches' is an idiom.
It means laughing so much that your sides hurt.
Answer: laughing a lot
quiz.mistake: Thinks of stitches from sewing or a doctor

quiz.q: Which spelling of the noun meaning 'the quality of being funny' is used in British and Indian English?
quiz.explain: British and Indian English write 'humour'. 'Humor' is the American spelling.
steps: British and Indian English write the noun as 'humour'.
'Humor' is American spelling; the others are misspellings.
Answer: humour
quiz.mistake: Uses the American spelling

quiz.q: Which sentence uses exaggeration to be funny?
options: My school bag weighs a tonne!
I carried my bag to school.
quiz.explain: No school bag weighs a tonne (1000 kg). Saying so is a funny exaggeration, also called hyperbole.
steps: Look for a claim that cannot be literally true.
No school bag weighs a tonne (1000 kg), so 'weighs a tonne!' is a funny exaggeration.
Answer: My school bag weighs a tonne!
quiz.mistake: Does not notice the impossible amount

quiz.q: What is an idiom?
options: A word that sounds like another word
A word with the opposite meaning
A phrase whose meaning differs from its separate words
quiz.explain: In an idiom the words together have a special meaning, like 'in stitches' meaning laughing a lot.
steps: An idiom's words together have a special meaning.
For example 'in stitches' means laughing a lot, not stitching.
Answer: A phrase whose meaning differs from its separate words
quiz.mistake: Confuses idioms with homophones or antonyms

quiz.q: Meera kept a straight face while Ravi made funny faces. What did Meera do?
quiz.explain: To keep a straight face is to stop yourself from laughing.
steps: To 'keep a straight face' means to stop yourself from laughing.
So Meera did not laugh.
Answer: She did not laugh
quiz.mistake: Takes 'straight' literally

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'funny'?
quiz.explain: Amusing means causing laughter or a smile, which is what funny means. The others are nearly opposites.
steps: A synonym has the same meaning.
Amusing means causing laughter, like funny; serious, gloomy and dull are nearly opposites.
Answer: Amusing
quiz.mistake: Picks an antonym instead of a synonym

quiz.q: Choose the correctly spelt adjective formed from 'humour'.
quiz.explain: Even in British English, the adjective drops the 'u': humorous.
steps: The noun is 'humour', but the adjective drops the 'u'.
The correct adjective is 'humorous'.
Answer: humorous
quiz.mistake: Keeps the 'u' from 'humour' in the adjective

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: My friend said he was 'pulling my leg', but my leg is fine! What is an idiom?
teach.praise: Hee hee! An idiom is a phrase with a special meaning, so he was only teasing me. My leg is safe!
teach.nudge: Do the words in an idiom mean exactly what they say? And what was my friend really doing?

revise.summary: Humour often comes from surprise, exaggeration and funny misunderstandings. Idioms have meanings different from their separate words, like 'pulling my leg', which means teasing.
focus: Know the meanings of humour idioms.
Spell 'humour' (British and Indian) and 'humorous' correctly.
Spot exaggeration used to be funny.
remember: An idiom is a group of words whose meaning is different from the meanings of the separate words.
crack a joke (tell a joke), in stitches (laughing a lot), keep a straight face (not laugh), tickled pink (very pleased), have the last laugh (win in the end after being doubted).
'Humour' is the British and Indian spelling; 'humor' is American. The adjective is 'humorous'.
traps: Don't take an idiom literally: 'in stitches' is not about sewing.
Don't keep the 'u' in the adjective: write 'humorous', not 'humourous'.

topics.title: Reported speech: telling what someone said

learn.hook: The king said something clever at dinner, and now the whole palace wants to know. How do you pass it on without quoting every word?
points: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks: Tenali said, "I am ready."
Reported (indirect) speech gives the meaning without quotation marks, often with 'that': Tenali said that he was ready.
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, asked, told), the tense usually moves one step back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, simple past → past perfect.
Pronouns and words of time and place change: I → he/she, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, now → then, this → that.
Questions use 'asked' with if/whether (yes/no questions) or the wh-word, in normal statement order: The king asked where Tenali was going. Commands use told/ordered + to: The king told him to sit.

example.q: Change to reported speech: The king said, "I will reward the wisest man tomorrow."
steps: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past, so the tense moves back: will → would.
The pronoun changes: I → he (the king).
The time word changes: tomorrow → the next day.
Remove the quotation marks and add 'that'.
example.answer: The king said that he would reward the wisest man the next day.

learn.reallife: News reporters use reported speech all the time: 'The minister said that the bridge would open soon.' You use it too when you tell your parents what your teacher said.

games.title: Statement, question or command?
items: "I love mangoes."
"Where is my pen?"
"Close the door."
"Are you coming?"
"We won the match."
"Sit down quietly."
"Do not run in the corridor."
"Who broke the vase?"
"The tea is ready."

quiz.q: Choose the correct reported speech: Ria said, "I am hungry."
options: Ria said that she was hungry.
Ria said that I am hungry.
Ria said that she is being hungry.
Ria asked that she was hungry.
quiz.explain: 'I' becomes 'she' and 'am' moves back to 'was' after 'said'.
steps: After 'said', change the pronoun and move the tense back.
'I' → 'she' and 'am' → 'was': Ria said that she was hungry.
Answer: Ria said that she was hungry.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the pronoun or the tense

quiz.q: The king asked, "Where are you going, Tenali?" Choose the correct reported speech.
options: The king asked Tenali where was he going.
The king asked Tenali where he was going.
The king said Tenali where he was going.
The king asked Tenali that where he is going.
quiz.explain: In a reported question the word order becomes like a statement (he was going), and there is no question mark.
steps: In a reported question the word order becomes like a statement and there is no question mark.
'Where are you going' → where he was going.
Answer: The king asked Tenali where he was going.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the question word order 'was he' in reported speech

quiz.q: Mother said to me, "Finish your homework." Choose the correct reported speech.
options: Mother said that I finish my homework.
Mother asked me if I finish my homework.
Mother told me finishing my homework.
Mother told me to finish my homework.
quiz.explain: A command is reported with 'told' + person + 'to' + verb.
steps: The sentence is a command.
A command is reported with told + person + to + verb: Mother told me to finish my homework.
Answer: Mother told me to finish my homework.
quiz.mistake: Reports a command like a statement or a question

quiz.q: In reported speech after 'said', the word 'tomorrow' usually changes to ___.
quiz.explain: By the time the words are reported, 'tomorrow' is no longer tomorrow, so it becomes 'the next day'.
steps: By the time the words are reported, 'tomorrow' has passed.
So 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day'.
Answer: the next day
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the change for 'tomorrow' with the change for 'yesterday'

quiz.q: Arjun asked me, "Can you help me?" Choose the correct reported speech.
options: Arjun asked if I could help him.
Arjun asked can I help him.
Arjun asked if I can helped him.
Arjun said if I could help him.
quiz.explain: A yes/no question uses 'asked if'. 'Can' moves back to 'could', 'you' becomes 'I' and 'me' becomes 'him'.
steps: A yes/no question is reported with 'asked if'.
'can' → 'could', 'you' → 'I', 'me' → 'him': Arjun asked if I could help him.
Answer: Arjun asked if I could help him.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the question form or uses 'said' for a question

quiz.q: Which sentence is in direct speech?
options: She said that she was tired.
They asked whether it was late.
quiz.explain: Direct speech gives the exact words inside quotation marks.
steps: Direct speech gives the speaker's exact words inside quotation marks.
Only 'Tenali said, "The jar is empty."' has quotation marks.
Answer: Tenali said, "The jar is empty."
quiz.mistake: Thinks any sentence with 'said' is direct speech

quiz.q: Raju said, "I can solve this riddle." Complete: Raju said that he ___ solve that riddle.
quiz.explain: After a past reporting verb, 'can' moves back to 'could'.
steps: The reporting verb 'said' is in the past.
So 'can' moves back to 'could'.
Answer: could
quiz.mistake: Does not shift the modal back in reported speech

quiz.q: A yes/no question is reported using which word(s)?
quiz.explain: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether': She asked if I was ready.
steps: Wh-questions keep their question word, but yes/no questions need a joining word.
That word is 'if' or 'whether'.
Answer: if or whether
quiz.mistake: Uses 'that', which is for reported statements

teach.ask: Gappu flutters: My friend said, "I am going to the fair." How do I tell Mum what he said without using his exact words?
teach.praise: Tweet! 'He said that he was going to the fair.' Change the pronoun and step the tense back. Easy!
teach.nudge: What happens to the tense after 'said'? And does 'I' stay 'I' when you report someone else's words?

revise.summary: Direct speech gives exact words in quotation marks; reported speech gives the meaning, often with 'that'. After a past reporting verb, tenses move back and pronouns, time and place words change.
focus: Change statements, questions and commands into reported speech.
Shift tenses back after said/asked/told.
Change pronouns and time/place words.
remember: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, simple past → past perfect.
today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before, here → there, now → then, this → that.
Questions: asked + if/whether or the wh-word, in statement order. Commands: told/ordered + to.
traps: Don't keep question word order: 'where he was going', not 'where was he going'.
Don't use 'that' for a yes/no question; use 'if' or 'whether'.
Don't forget to change the pronoun and the tense: 'Ria said that she was hungry.'

topics.title: Humorous poems: rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration

learn.hook: Can a paratha be used as a brick? In a funny poem, anything can happen!
points: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words and their meanings.
Rhyme: words that end with the same sound, like thick and brick. A rhyme scheme labels line endings with letters: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme; ABAB means lines 1-3 and 2-4 rhyme.
Rhythm is the beat of a poem, made by the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables. A bouncy rhythm makes a funny poem fun to read aloud.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect: 'I've told you a million times!'
Onomatopoeia is a word that imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash). Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words (Bunty bought big balloons).

example.q: Read this original poem: 'Our cook made parathas so heavy and thick, / Our dog used one as a brand-new brick. / Papa took a bite and his jaw went CRACK! / Now he wants his teeth and his money back!' Think it through: what is the rhyme scheme, and where is the exaggeration?
steps: Line endings: thick (A), brick (A), crack (B), back (B).
So the rhyme scheme is AABB.
No real paratha could be used as a brick: that is hyperbole.
'CRACK' imitates a sound, so it is onomatopoeia that adds to the fun.
example.answer: The rhyme scheme is AABB, and the paratha-as-a-brick line is hyperbole.

learn.reallife: Advertising jingles, cricket chants and birthday rhymes use rhyme, rhythm and exaggeration to stick in your memory.

games.title: Name the trick
items: I've told you a million times!
The thunder went boom.
Seven silly snakes slithered.
The old door went creak.
I'm so hungry I could eat an elephant.

quiz.q: Read: 'Our cook made parathas so heavy and thick, / Our dog used one as a brand-new brick.' Which two words rhyme?
quiz.explain: Rhyming words end with the same sound: thick and brick both end in '-ick'.
steps: Rhyming words end with the same sound.
The line-endings 'thick' and 'brick' both end in '-ick'.
Answer: thick, brick
quiz.mistake: Looks for words that share letters at the start instead of sounds at the end

quiz.q: A four-line stanza has lines 1 and 2 rhyming and lines 3 and 4 rhyming. What is its rhyme scheme?
quiz.explain: The first two lines share sound A, the next two share sound B: AABB.
steps: Lines 1 and 2 share one sound (A); lines 3 and 4 share another (B).
So the rhyme scheme is AABB.
Answer: AABB
quiz.mistake: Mixes up couplets (AABB) with alternate rhyme (ABAB)

quiz.q: Read: 'Papa took a bite and his jaw went CRACK!' The word 'CRACK' is an example of ___.
quiz.explain: 'Crack' imitates the sound it names, which is onomatopoeia.
steps: 'CRACK' imitates the sound it names.
A word that imitates a sound is onomatopoeia.
Answer: onomatopoeia
quiz.mistake: Thinks any figure of speech in a poem is a simile or metaphor

quiz.q: Which line uses hyperbole?
options: Our dog used the paratha as a brand-new brick.
quiz.explain: A paratha cannot really be used as a brick. This deliberate exaggeration is hyperbole.
steps: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration.
A paratha cannot really be used as a brick, so that line is hyperbole.
Answer: Our dog used the paratha as a brand-new brick.
quiz.mistake: Does not separate an ordinary description from an exaggeration

quiz.q: Which line has alliteration?
options: I like to read at night.
Peter's pet parrot plays the piano.
The rain fell on the roof.
quiz.explain: The 'p' sound repeats at the start of Peter's, pet, parrot, plays and piano.
steps: Alliteration repeats the same first sound in nearby words.
'Peter's pet parrot plays the piano' repeats 'p'.
Answer: Peter's pet parrot plays the piano.
quiz.mistake: Thinks alliteration means rhyme at the end of lines

quiz.q: What is hyperbole?
options: A word that imitates a sound
A word with the same meaning
quiz.explain: Hyperbole means exaggerating on purpose, often to be funny or to stress a point.
steps: Hyperbole means exaggerating on purpose.
A comparison with like/as is a simile; a sound word is onomatopoeia.
Answer: A deliberate exaggeration
quiz.mistake: Confuses hyperbole with simile or onomatopoeia

quiz.q: Which word rhymes with 'laugh'?
quiz.explain: 'Laugh' and 'half' end with the same sound '-af', even though they are spelt differently.
steps: Rhyme depends on sound, not spelling.
'Laugh' and 'half' both end with the sound '-af'.
Answer: half
quiz.mistake: Matches the first letter or the spelling instead of the ending sound

quiz.q: In the rhyme scheme ABAB, which lines rhyme?
quiz.explain: The letter A marks lines 1 and 3; the letter B marks lines 2 and 4. Lines with the same letter rhyme.
steps: Lines with the same letter rhyme.
In ABAB, A = lines 1 and 3, B = lines 2 and 4.
Answer: Lines 1 and 3, lines 2 and 4
quiz.mistake: Reads ABAB as pairs of neighbouring lines

teach.ask: Gappu giggles: Why is a poem about a paratha used as a brick so funny? What tricks does the poet use?
teach.praise: Ha! Big exaggeration, bouncy rhymes and sound words like CRACK. That is why funny poems are fun!
teach.nudge: Could a paratha really be a brick? What do we call that? And what do the line endings do?

revise.summary: 'A Concrete Example' is a humorous poem that has fun with words. We learn rhyme, rhyme scheme, rhythm, hyperbole, onomatopoeia and alliteration.
focus: Find rhyming words by their ending sound.
Work out AABB and ABAB rhyme schemes.
Spot hyperbole, onomatopoeia and alliteration.
remember: AABB means lines 1-2 rhyme and lines 3-4 rhyme; ABAB means lines 1-3 and 2-4 rhyme.
Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Onomatopoeia imitates a sound (crack, buzz, splash); alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words.
traps: Rhyme is about the ending sound, not the spelling or first letter: 'laugh' rhymes with 'half'.
Don't read ABAB as pairs of neighbouring lines.
Alliteration is not rhyme at the end of lines.

topics.title: Fun with language: puns, homophones and homonyms

learn.hook: Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school! Words with two meanings make the best jokes.
points: A pun is a joke that plays on a word with two meanings, or on two words that sound alike.
The title 'A Concrete Example' can be read two ways: 'concrete' means real and specific, and it is also the building material made of cement, sand, gravel and water.
Homophones sound the same but have different spellings and meanings: flour/flower, pair/pear, knight/night, peace/piece, weather/whether, stationary/stationery.
Homonyms have the same spelling and sound but different meanings: bat (cricket bat / flying animal), bank (money bank / river bank), bark (a dog's bark / a tree's bark).
Literal meaning is the plain meaning of the words; figurative meaning is a special or imaginative meaning. 'A piece of cake' literally is cake, but figuratively means 'very easy'.

example.q: Think it through: 'Why did the student carry a ladder to class? She wanted to go to high school!' Explain the pun.
steps: Find the word or phrase with two meanings: 'high school'.
Meaning 1: a level of school for older students.
Meaning 2: a school that is high up, so you would need a ladder.
The joke works because both meanings fit at once.
example.answer: 'High school' means a senior school and also, jokingly, a school that is high up, which is why she needs a ladder.

learn.reallife: Newspaper headlines, shop names and greeting cards love puns, like a tailor's shop called 'Sew Good' (it sounds like 'so good'). Spotting them makes reading more fun.

quiz.q: Which pair are homophones?
quiz.explain: Flour and flower sound the same but have different spellings and meanings.

quiz.q: 'The dog's bark woke me' and 'The tree's bark is rough.' Here 'bark' is a ___.
quiz.explain: The same word, spelt and said the same way, has two different meanings. That is a homonym.
steps: 'Bark' is spelt and said the same way in both sentences but means two things.
A word like that is a homonym.
Answer: homonym

quiz.q: Why is this a pun? 'I tried to be a baker, but I couldn't make enough dough.'
options: 'Dough' means bread mixture and is also slang for money
quiz.explain: A baker makes dough (the mixture), and 'dough' is also an informal word for money. Both meanings work together.

In 'Your answer is right', it means correct.

topics.title: Folk wisdom tales, morals and proverbs

learn.hook: Two brothers, one big basket of mangoes and a fight that could last forever. Can one wise sentence fix it?
points: The lesson 'Wisdom Paves the Way' is a folk story in which clear, wise thinking opens a way out of a difficult problem.

Folk tales are stories passed down by word of mouth over many generations, so their first authors are usually unknown. India has a rich storytelling tradition, including folk tales and well-loved fable collections like the Panchatantra.
Folk tales often have a simple setting, a problem, a wise or clever character, and a moral, which is the lesson the story teaches.
A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice: 'Look before you leap', 'A stitch in time saves nine', 'Two heads are better than one'.
'Wisdom' is a noun. Its adjective is 'wise' and its adverb is 'wisely'.

example.q: Read this original tale: Two brothers in a Rajasthan village quarrelled over a basket of mangoes left by their grandfather. Each said the other would cheat. Old Gomti-ma listened and said, "Let one of you divide the mangoes into two heaps, and let the other choose first." The quarrel ended at once. Think it through: why does her plan make the sharing fair?
steps: One brother divides; the other picks first.
If the divider makes one heap smaller, the other brother will take the bigger heap.
So the divider is forced to make the two heaps as equal as he can.
Neither brother can complain: one made the heaps, the other chose.
example.answer: The divider must make equal heaps, because any bigger heap would be chosen by the other brother.

learn.reallife: When two friends share a samosa, one cuts and the other chooses. You are using Gomti-ma's wisdom!

games.title: Folk tales: true or false?

A proverb is a long story with many characters.
A proverb is a short, well-known saying, not a story.
In Gomti-ma's plan, the same brother both divides and chooses.
One brother divides and the other chooses first. That is what makes it fair.
The Panchatantra is a well-known collection of Indian animal fables.
Its stories use animals to teach lessons about wise living.
The adjective form of 'wisdom' is 'wise'.
Wisdom (noun), wise (adjective), wisely (adverb).

steps: To 'pave the way' is to prepare a path so something can happen.
So 'wisdom paves the way' means wisdom makes something possible or easier.
Answer: Makes something possible or easier
quiz.mistake: Takes 'pave' only in its literal sense of laying a road

quiz.q: What is the adjective form of 'wisdom'?
quiz.explain: 'Wise' describes a person, so it is the adjective. 'Wisely' is the adverb.
steps: 'Wisdom' is the noun; the word that describes a person is the adjective.
That adjective is 'wise' ('wisely' is the adverb).
Answer: wise
quiz.mistake: Confuses the adjective with the adverb

quiz.q: Which of these is a proverb?
quiz.explain: 'Look before you leap' is a short traditional saying that gives advice: think before you act.
steps: A proverb is a short traditional saying that gives advice.
'Look before you leap' advises thinking before acting; the others are ordinary sentences.
Answer: Look before you leap.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any short sentence is a proverb

quiz.q: Folk tales were mostly passed on ___.
quiz.explain: Folk tales come from times before printing, when people told stories aloud.
steps: Folk tales come from times before printing.
People told them aloud, so they passed by word of mouth.
Answer: by word of mouth
quiz.mistake: Forgets that folk tales are older than modern media

quiz.q: Which proverb fits? Meena got a small leak in the roof fixed before the monsoon, so the room stayed dry all season.
options: A stitch in time saves nine
Too many cooks spoil the broth
All that glitters is not gold
Slow and steady wins the race
quiz.explain: Fixing a small problem early stopped a bigger one later. That is what 'a stitch in time saves nine' means.
steps: Meena fixed a small leak early, so a bigger problem never came.
That is the meaning of 'A stitch in time saves nine'.
Answer: A stitch in time saves nine

quiz.q: What do we call the lesson that a story teaches?
quiz.explain: The moral is the lesson. The setting is the time and place of the story.
steps: The lesson a story teaches is its moral.
The setting is the time and place, not the lesson.
Answer: The moral
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the moral with the setting

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'wise'?
quiz.explain: A wise person and a sensible person both show good judgement. The other words mean the opposite.
steps: A synonym has nearly the same meaning.
'Sensible' shows good judgement like 'wise'; foolish, careless and rash are opposites.
Answer: Sensible
quiz.mistake: Chooses an antonym instead of a synonym

teach.ask: Gappu asks: What is a folk tale, and what is the moral in a story like Gomti-ma's?
teach.praise: Hoot hoot! A folk tale is an old story passed down by telling, and its moral is the wise lesson inside it.
teach.nudge: How did folk tales travel before books? And what do we call the lesson a story gives?

focus: Explain why a wise solution works, like 'one divides, the other chooses'.
Know the features of a folk tale and what a moral is.
Match a proverb to a situation.
remember: A proverb is a short, well-known saying that gives advice: 'Look before you leap', 'A stitch in time saves nine', 'Two heads are better than one'.
The moral is the lesson the story teaches.
wisdom (noun), wise (adjective), wisely (adverb).
traps: Don't mix up the moral (lesson) with the setting (time and place).
Don't confuse the adjective 'wise' with the adverb 'wisely'.
Don't pick a familiar proverb without matching its meaning.

topics.title: Problem solving: steps and linking words

learn.hook: A wise person does not panic. She goes step by step. And when we explain steps, little linking words do a big job!
points: Problem solving has clear steps: understand the problem, think of possible solutions, choose the best one, try it out, and check whether it worked.
Sequence connectors show the order of steps: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Cause and effect connectors join a reason and a result: because, as, so, therefore, as a result. 'Because' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result.
Contrast connectors show a difference or surprise: but, however, although, though.

example.q: Think it through: The plants in Class 8's garden dry up every summer holiday. Explain how to solve this using connectors.
steps: First, understand the problem: no one waters the plants during the holidays.
Next, list solutions: a watering rota, a drip bottle, or moving pots to shade.
Then, choose the best one: a rota of students who live nearby, because it is simple and free.
Finally, check after the holidays whether the plants survived.
example.answer: First understand, next list ideas, then choose and try the best one, and finally check the result.

learn.reallife: Recipes, science experiments and instructions for a board game all use sequence words like first, then and finally.

games.title: Steps to solve a problem
games.prompt: Put the problem-solving steps in order

Think of possible solutions

Try it out

items.text: ___, read the question carefully.

quiz.q: Which word shows the LAST step in a sequence?
quiz.explain: 'Finally' tells the reader that this is the last step.
steps: Sequence words: First → Next → Then → Finally.
'Finally' marks the last step.
Answer: Finally
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'then' marks the end

quiz.q: Choose the connector: The well was dry, ___ the villagers dug a new one.
quiz.explain: The dry well is the reason; digging a new one is the result. 'So' introduces a result.
steps: The dry well is the reason; digging a new one is the result.
A result is introduced by 'so'.
Answer: so
quiz.mistake: Uses 'because', which introduces a reason, not a result

quiz.q: Which sentence shows cause and effect?
options: It rained heavily, so the match was called off.
Rani is tall but her brother is short.
quiz.explain: Heavy rain (cause) led to the match being called off (effect), joined by 'so'.
steps: Cause and effect means one thing makes another happen.
Heavy rain (cause) → match called off (effect), joined by 'so'.
Answer: It rained heavily, so the match was called off.
quiz.mistake: Confuses contrast ('but') with cause and effect

quiz.q: What should you do FIRST when solving a problem?
quiz.explain: You cannot choose a good solution until you understand the problem.
steps: You cannot choose a good solution without knowing the problem.
So the first step is to understand what the problem is.
Answer: Understand what the problem is
quiz.mistake: Rushes to a solution before understanding the problem

quiz.q: 'Although the path was steep, the children kept climbing.' The word 'although' shows ___.
quiz.explain: 'Although' shows something surprising: the path was hard, yet they kept going.
steps: The path was steep, yet the children kept climbing — a surprising contrast.
'Although' shows contrast.
Answer: contrast
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'although' shows a reason

quiz.q: Pick the best order: (a) Water the seed (b) Dig a small hole (c) Put the seed in (d) Cover it with soil
quiz.explain: You dig the hole, place the seed, cover it with soil and then water it.
steps: Think of the real order: dig a hole (b), put the seed in (c), cover with soil (d), then water (a).
So the order is b, c, d, a.
Answer: b, c, d, a
quiz.mistake: Keeps the order in which the steps are listed instead of the logical order

quiz.q: In a sentence, the connector 'because' introduces ___.
quiz.explain: 'Because' answers 'why?': We stayed in because it rained.
steps: 'Because' answers the question 'why?'.
So it introduces a reason.
Answer: a reason
quiz.mistake: Mixes up 'because' (reason) with 'so' (result)

quiz.q: Choose the best connector: 'Ravi missed the bus. ___, he was late for school.'
quiz.explain: Being late is the result of missing the bus, so 'As a result' fits.
steps: Being late for school happened because Ravi missed the bus.
A connector for a result is 'As a result'.
Answer: As a result
quiz.mistake: Puts 'because' before the result instead of before the reason

teach.ask: Gappu is stuck: My nest keeps falling apart! How should I solve this problem, and which words help me explain the steps?
teach.praise: First understand, then try ideas, finally check. And words like 'first', 'then' and 'finally' show the order. My nest will be strong!
teach.nudge: What is the very first step? Which little words show the order of steps? And what do you do at the end?

revise.summary: Problem solving has clear steps: understand the problem, think of solutions, choose the best, try it and check. Connectors show sequence, cause and effect, and contrast.
focus: Order the steps of solving a problem.
Use sequence connectors: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Choose cause-effect and contrast connectors correctly.
remember: Cause and effect: because, as, so, therefore, as a result. 'Because' introduces the reason; 'so' introduces the result.
Contrast: but, however, although, though.
Sequence: first, next, then, after that, finally.
traps: Don't mix up 'because' (reason) with 'so' (result).
'Although' shows contrast, not a reason.
Don't rush to a solution before understanding the problem.

topics.title: Phrasal verbs for solving problems

learn.hook: 'Give up', 'give in', 'give away': change one little word and the meaning flips! Meet phrasal verbs.
points: A phrasal verb is a verb followed by a particle (a small word such as up, out, into, on, off) that together have a new meaning.

Problem-solving phrasal verbs: figure out (understand or solve), work out (find the answer), come up with (think of an idea), look into (investigate), sort out (fix), carry on (continue), give up (stop trying).
Changing the particle changes the meaning: give up (stop trying), give in (accept defeat), give away (hand out for free).
More useful ones: put off (postpone), look after (take care of), run out of (have none left), find out (discover), turn down (refuse).

example.q: Think it through: Replace the words in brackets with a phrasal verb. 'Tara (thought of) a clever plan to save water in the school.'
steps: The meaning is 'produced an idea'.
The phrasal verb for producing an idea is 'come up with'.
The sentence is in the past, so use 'came up with'.
example.answer: Tara came up with a clever plan to save water in the school.

learn.reallife: Everyday English is full of phrasal verbs: 'Switch off the fan', 'Pick up your bag', 'We ran out of sugar'.

quiz.explain: 'Give up' means to stop trying.
steps: 'Give up' is a phrasal verb.
In 'Don't give up', it means stop trying.

quiz.q: Choose the phrasal verb: Meera ___ a smart way to share the mangoes.
quiz.explain: 'Came up with' means thought of an idea. 'Came down with' means fell ill.
steps: 'Come up with' means to think of an idea; 'come down with' means to fall ill.
Meera thought of a smart way, so she 'came up with' it.
Answer: came up with
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that the particle changes the meaning

quiz.q: Which phrasal verb means 'to investigate'?

steps: 'Look into' means to examine something carefully.
'Look after' is take care of; 'look up to' is respect; 'look down on' is think less of.
Answer: look into
quiz.mistake: Picks any 'look' phrasal verb without checking the meaning

quiz.q: 'The school trip was put off because of the rain.' Here 'put off' means ___.
quiz.explain: 'Put off' means moved to a later time, which is postponed.
steps: The trip did not happen on that day because of rain.
'Put off' means postponed (moved to a later time).
Answer: postponed
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'put off' means cancelled for good

quiz.q: Which sentence means 'We had no milk left'?
quiz.explain: To run out of something is to use it all up so none is left.
steps: 'Run out of' means to use something up so none is left.
So 'We ran out of milk' means we had no milk left.
Answer: We ran out of milk.
quiz.mistake: Picks another 'run' phrasal verb with a different meaning

quiz.q: 'Please look after my tulsi plant while I am away.' Here 'look after' means ___.
quiz.explain: To look after something is to take care of it.
steps: 'Look after' means to take care of.
So you are asked to take care of the tulsi plant.
Answer: take care of
quiz.mistake: Thinks 'after' here is about place or time

quiz.q: Which of these means 'to hand out for free'?
quiz.explain: 'Give away' means to give something for free. 'Give up' is stop trying; 'give in' is accept defeat.
steps: 'Give up' = stop trying; 'give in' = accept defeat.
'Give away' = hand out for free.
Answer: give away
quiz.mistake: Does not notice that each particle gives a different meaning

quiz.q: A phrasal verb is made of ___.
options: a verb plus a particle such as up, out or into
a verb plus a suffix such as -ing
quiz.explain: Examples: give + up, look + into, run + out of. The words together carry a new meaning.
steps: Look at examples: give + up, look + into, run + out of.

teach.praise: Wow! A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, and that small word changes the whole meaning!
teach.nudge: What is added after 'give'? And does that small word change the meaning or keep it the same?

revise.summary: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle such as up, out, into, on or off, which together have a new meaning. Changing the particle changes the meaning.
focus: Know problem-solving phrasal verbs and their meanings.
Notice how the particle changes the meaning: give up, give in, give away.

remember: figure out (understand or solve), work out (find the answer), come up with (think of an idea), look into (investigate), sort out (fix), carry on (continue), give up (stop trying).
give up (stop trying), give in (accept defeat), give away (hand out for free).
put off (postpone), look after (take care of), run out of (have none left), find out (discover), turn down (refuse).
traps: Don't read the two words separately; they work as one meaning.
'Put off' means postponed, not cancelled for good.
Don't pick any 'look' or 'run' phrasal verb without checking the particle.

chapters.title: A Tale of Valour: Major Somnath Sharma and the Battle of Badgam

topics.title: Major Somnath Sharma: the first Param Vir Chakra

learn.hook: India's highest award for bravery has a very special first name on its list. Whose is it, and what did he do?
points: The lesson is a true account of courage: how Major Somnath Sharma led his soldiers in the Battle of Badgam.
The Param Vir Chakra (PVC) is India's highest military award for gallantry, given for the greatest bravery in the face of the enemy.
Major Somnath Sharma of the 4th Battalion of the Kumaon Regiment was the first-ever recipient of the Param Vir Chakra.

The Battle of Badgam was fought on 3 November 1947, near Srinagar in Jammu and Kashmir. His company held its position against a much larger attacking force until more troops arrived, helping to protect the Srinagar airfield.
He gave his life in this battle, so he received the award posthumously, which means after his death.

example.q: Read this original tribute: 'His arm was in a plaster cast, yet he would not stay behind. At Badgam he moved from post to post, cheering his men and guiding them, and he did not leave his position.' Think it through: what does this tell us about his character?
steps: Notice the injury: his arm was in a plaster cast.
Notice what he did anyway: he went with his men and moved from post to post.
Notice how he treated his soldiers: he cheered and guided them.
Put it together: he was brave, dutiful and a caring leader.
example.answer: He was courageous and devoted to duty, and he led and encouraged his men even when he was injured.

learn.reallife: The National War Memorial in New Delhi honours India's brave soldiers, including Param Vir Chakra recipients like Major Somnath Sharma.

topics.title: Courage: vocabulary and abstract nouns

learn.hook: You cannot hold courage in your hand, put it in your bag or weigh it. So what kind of noun is it?
points: Words close in meaning to courage: bravery, valour, gallantry, heroism, fearlessness. Opposites: cowardice, timidity, fearfulness.
An abstract noun names a quality, feeling or idea that we cannot see or touch: courage, honesty, freedom, kindness, loyalty.
Many abstract nouns come from adjectives: brave → bravery, loyal → loyalty, strong → strength, proud → pride, wise → wisdom, free → freedom, kind → kindness.
Some come from common nouns or verbs: hero → heroism, friend → friendship and decide → decision.
Courage is not only for soldiers. Telling the truth, standing up for someone who is being teased, or trying again after failing also takes courage.

example.q: Think it through: Find the abstract nouns in this sentence: 'The soldier's bravery and loyalty earned the respect of the whole nation.'
steps: Check each noun: soldier, bravery, loyalty, respect, nation.
A soldier and a nation can be seen, so they are not abstract.
Bravery, loyalty and respect are qualities or feelings that cannot be touched.
example.answer: bravery, loyalty, respect

learn.reallife: The Pradhan Mantri Rashtriya Bal Puraskar honours children for achievements that include bravery, such as saving someone in danger.

topics.title: Telling a true story: past tenses

learn.hook: A true story already happened. To tell it clearly, you need the right past tense at the right moment.
points: Simple past tells a completed action at a definite time: The battle began at dawn. We watched the parade yesterday.
Past continuous (was/were + verb-ing) shows an action in progress in the past: The soldiers were guarding the airfield.
Past continuous + simple past shows a longer action interrupted by a shorter one: We were eating dinner when the lights went off.
Past perfect (had + past participle) shows an action completed before another past action: The film had started when we reached the hall.
Learn irregular verbs: fight-fought-fought, hold-held-held, lead-led-led, give-gave-given, win-won-won, write-wrote-written.

example.q: Think it through: Join these two sentences using the past perfect. 'The match finished. Then we reached the stadium.'
steps: Find the earlier action: the match finished.
The earlier action takes the past perfect: had finished.
The later action stays in simple past: reached.
Join them with 'when'.
example.answer: The match had finished when we reached the stadium.

learn.reallife: Diaries, news reports and history books use past tenses to tell what happened, what was happening, and what had already happened.

quiz.explain: Was + writing (verb-ing) shows an action in progress in the past.

Answer: She was writing a poem.
quiz.mistake: Confuses past continuous with simple past or past perfect

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: The film ___ when we reached the hall.

steps: The film started before we reached — two past actions.
The earlier one takes the past perfect: had started.
Answer: had started

steps: 'Were digging' is past continuous — a longer action already going on.
The rain began and interrupted it.
Answer: Digging the garden
quiz.mistake: Thinks the simple past action was the longer one

quiz.q: Which tense shows an action completed before another past action?
quiz.explain: The past perfect (had + past participle) marks the earlier of two past actions.
steps: Two past actions: the earlier one takes had + past participle.
That is the past perfect tense.
Answer: Past perfect
quiz.mistake: Thinks the past continuous shows the earlier action

quiz.q: Fill in the blank: Yesterday, the students ___ the national flag at dawn.
quiz.explain: 'Yesterday' is a definite past time, so the simple past 'hoisted' is correct.
steps: 'Yesterday' names a definite past time.
A definite past time takes the simple past: hoisted.
Answer: hoisted
quiz.mistake: Uses the present perfect with a definite past time

quiz.q: Choose the correct option: While I ___ my homework, the lights went off.
quiz.explain: Homework was in progress when a shorter action interrupted it, so use past continuous.
steps: Doing homework was in progress when the shorter action (lights went off) happened.
A longer past action in progress takes the past continuous: was doing.
Answer: was doing
quiz.mistake: Uses simple past for the longer, interrupted action

quiz.q: What is the past participle of 'give'?
quiz.explain: give-gave-given. 'Gave' is the simple past; 'given' is the past participle, used with 'had' or 'has'.
steps: The forms are give – gave – given.
The past participle (used with had/has) is 'given'.
Answer: given
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple past form where the past participle is needed

teach.praise: Chirp! 'Was flying' is past continuous for something going on, and 'had flown' is past perfect for something done before another past action.
teach.nudge: Which helping verb shows an action in progress? Which helping verb shows an action that happened earlier?

revise.summary: To tell a true story we use simple past, past continuous and past perfect. Past continuous shows an action in progress, often interrupted by a simple past action; past perfect shows the earlier of two past actions.
focus: Choose the right past tense from the meaning.
Join two past actions with past perfect for the earlier one.
Learn irregular verb forms.
remember: Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing. Past perfect: had + past participle.
'We were eating dinner when the lights went off.'
fight-fought-fought, hold-held-held, lead-led-led, give-gave-given, win-won-won, write-wrote-written.
traps: Don't add -ed to an irregular verb: 'led', not 'leaded'.
Don't use simple past for the longer, interrupted action: 'While I was doing my homework'.
Don't use 'gave' where the past participle 'given' is needed.

topics.title: A poem on kindness: reading and figurative language

learn.hook: One small act on a crowded bus can warm a whole crowd. Poems know how to show that.
points: 'Somebody's Mother' is a poem about kindness to an elderly person. Its theme: every elder is somebody's dear one, so treat them as you would treat your own family.
The theme is the main idea of a poem. The speaker is the voice telling the poem. A stanza is a group of lines in a poem.
A simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as': warm as sunshine. A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as': his smile was a lamp.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things: The old bus groaned up the hill.
Empathy means imagining how another person feels. Kind actions often begin with empathy.

example.q: Read this original poem: 'The bus was full, the seats were gone, / An old man held the rail alone; / A schoolgirl stood and gave her place, / A thank-you bloomed upon his face. / "He's someone's grandpa, just like mine," / She thought, and the bus felt warm as sunshine.' Think it through: find one metaphor and one simile.
steps: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
'A thank-you bloomed upon his face' compares his grateful smile to a flower opening: metaphor.
A simile uses 'like' or 'as'.
'warm as sunshine' compares the bus's feeling to sunshine using 'as': simile.
example.answer: Metaphor: 'A thank-you bloomed upon his face'. Simile: 'warm as sunshine'.

learn.reallife: Giving your seat to an elder in a bus or metro, or helping a neighbour carry vegetables, is the kindness this poem celebrates.

remember: The theme is the main idea of a poem; a stanza is a group of lines in a poem.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.
Empathy means imagining how another person feels.
traps: Don't call every comparison a simile; without 'like' or 'as' it is a metaphor.
Don't confuse personification with simile: 'The old bus groaned' is personification.
A group of lines in a poem is a stanza, not a paragraph.

topics.title: Respect for elders: polite language and modals

learn.hook: 'Give me water!' or 'Could you please pass me some water?' Same request, very different respect!
points: Modals are helping verbs that show ability, permission, advice, offers and more: can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must.
Polite requests: Could you...? Would you...? 'Could you please help me?' sounds more polite than 'Can you help me?'
Asking permission: May I...? (formal, very polite) or Can I...? (informal). 'May I come in, ma'am?'
Offering help: Shall I...? Would you like...? 'Shall I carry your bag, Dadi?' Giving advice: should. 'You should rest, Nanaji.'
Respect also shows in words like please, thank you and sorry, in a gentle tone, and in listening patiently when elders speak.

example.q: Think it through: Make this more polite and respectful: 'Uncle, move your bag. I want to sit.'
steps: Start with a polite modal for a request: Could you...
Add 'please'.
Explain the need gently instead of demanding.
Thank the person.
example.answer: Uncle, could you please move your bag a little so that I can sit? Thank you!

learn.reallife: At a family wedding or a visit to Nani's house, polite phrases like 'May I help?' and 'Shall I bring you tea?' make elders feel cared for.

quiz.q: 'Shall I bring you a glass of water, Nani?' The speaker is ___.

steps: 'Shall I...?' is used to offer to do something for someone.

quiz.q: Which modal gives advice?
quiz.explain: 'You should rest' gives advice. 'Can' shows ability or informal permission.

'Can' shows ability or informal permission.

quiz.q: 'When Dadaji was young, he ___ climb coconut trees.' Choose the modal for past ability.
quiz.explain: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' and shows ability in the past.
steps: The sentence is about the past ('When Dadaji was young').
Past ability uses 'could', the past of 'can'.
Answer: could
quiz.mistake: Uses present-tense 'can' for a past ability

quiz.q: Which sentence shows respect to an elder?

quiz.explain: Offering a hand gently is caring and respectful. The others are impatient or rude.

quiz.q: Which modal shows a rule in this museum sign? 'Visitors ___ not touch the paintings.'

Answer: must

quiz.q: Which word is a synonym of 'respect'?
quiz.explain: To honour someone is to show them great respect.
steps: A synonym of respect means showing high regard.

chapters.title: Verghese Kurien — I Too Had A Dream

topics.title: Verghese Kurien and the White Revolution

learn.hook: India once did not have enough milk for its children. Today it produces more milk than any other country. Who dreamed this big?
points: The lesson tells the story of Dr Verghese Kurien, whose dream was to make dairy farmers prosper. 'I Too Had a Dream' is also the title of his memoir.
Verghese Kurien was born on 26 November 1921 in Kozhikode (Calicut), Kerala. In 1949 he was posted to Anand in Gujarat, where he chose to stay and work with dairy farmers.
He is called the 'Father of the White Revolution'. The White Revolution was the huge rise in India's milk production.
Operation Flood, launched in 1970 by the National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) under his leadership, linked village milk producers to cities across India. Kurien was the first chairman of the NDDB.
Today India is the world's largest producer of milk, and his birthday, 26 November, is celebrated as National Milk Day.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'Kurien was an engineer, not a farmer. Yet when he saw how farmers in Anand got very little money for their milk, he decided to stay and help them. He believed that if farmers owned their own dairy, they would get a fair price.' Think it through: what was Kurien's dream?
steps: Notice the problem: farmers got very little money for their milk.
Notice his decision: he stayed in Anand to help them.
Notice his belief: farmers should own their dairy to get a fair price.
So his dream was about fairness and farmers' prosperity.
example.answer: His dream was that dairy farmers would own and run their own dairies and get a fair price for their milk.

learn.reallife: The packet of milk or curd that reaches your home every morning is part of a supply chain that grew out of the White Revolution.

topics.title: Amul and the cooperative way

learn.hook: What happens when thousands of farmers who each own just one or two buffaloes join hands? They build one of India's biggest dairies!
points: A cooperative is a group owned and run by its members for their shared benefit. Each member has a say (one member, one vote) and profits are shared among members.
In 1946, dairy farmers of Kaira (Kheda) district formed the Kaira District Cooperative Milk Producers' Union at Anand, Gujarat, led by Tribhuvandas Patel. Its products later took the brand name Amul.
Amul is often explained as 'Anand Milk Union Limited'. Kurien worked with this union and helped it grow.
The 'Anand pattern' has three levels: village dairy cooperative societies collect milk, a district union processes it, and a state federation markets it.
Because the farmers own the system, middlemen are removed and farmers receive a fairer price for their milk.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'Every morning and evening, Lakshmiben carries her buffalo's milk to the village society. The milk is tested for fat, and she is paid according to its quality. At the end of the year, she also gets a share of the profit, because she is a member.' Think it through: why is this a cooperative?
steps: Lakshmiben is a member, not just a seller.
She is paid fairly, by the quality of her milk.
Profits are shared with members like her.
Ownership and benefit belong to the members: that is a cooperative.
example.answer: It is a cooperative because the farmers are members who own it, are paid fairly and share its profits.

topics.title: Describing a process: active and passive voice

learn.hook: 'The farmer milks the buffalo' or 'The buffalo is milked'? Both are correct. The choice depends on what you want to highlight.
points: In the active voice, the subject does the action: The society collects the milk.
In the passive voice, the receiver of the action becomes the subject: The milk is collected by the society.
Passive = a form of 'be' + past participle. Present: is/are collected. Past: was/were collected. Future: will be collected. Present continuous: is being collected. With modals: can be collected.
The doer is shown with 'by' (by the society), or left out when it is unknown or unimportant: The milk is pasteurised and packed.
The passive is common when describing processes, because the steps matter more than who does them.

example.q: Think it through: Change to the passive voice: 'The workers packed the milk in pouches.'
steps: Object of the active sentence: the milk. It becomes the subject.
The verb 'packed' is simple past, so use was/were + past participle: was packed.
Add the doer with 'by': by the workers.
Keep the rest: in pouches.
example.answer: The milk was packed in pouches by the workers.

chapters.title: The Case of the Fifth Word

topics.title: Mystery stories: clues, suspects and red herrings

learn.hook: The last gulab jamun has vanished from the fridge. Three suspects, one sticky clue. Ready, detective?
points: 'The Case of the Fifth Word' is a mystery story in which a puzzle is solved by careful observation and logical thinking.
A mystery story usually has: a puzzle or crime, a detective, suspects, clues, at least one false lead, and a final reveal where the solution is explained.

Key words: clue (a sign that helps solve a puzzle), suspect (a person who may be guilty), culprit (the person who actually did it), alibi (proof that a suspect was somewhere else), motive (the reason for doing it), witness (someone who saw something), evidence (facts or objects that show what happened).
A red herring is a misleading clue that points the reader the wrong way.
A good detective separates facts from guesses and checks every clue.

example.q: Read this original mystery: 'The last gulab jamun vanished from the Iyer family's fridge. Grandma said, "I was at the market all evening," and the shopkeeper agreed. Kavya pointed at the cat, but the fridge door was too heavy for a cat to open. Detective Divya then spotted sweet syrup on her brother Ravi's homework book.' Think it through: who is the likely culprit, and what is the red herring?
steps: Grandma has an alibi: the shopkeeper confirms she was at the market.
The cat is suggested, but it could not open the heavy fridge door: that is the red herring.
The syrup on Ravi's book is evidence that links him to the sweet.
So Ravi is the likely culprit.
example.answer: Ravi is the likely culprit. The cat is the red herring.

learn.reallife: Detective stories like the Feluda tales by Satyajit Ray and the Byomkesh Bakshi stories are loved across India because readers try to solve the case before the detective does.

topics.title: Logical deduction and inference

learn.hook: A secret message is hidden in plain sight. Only a careful reader will find it!
points: An inference is a conclusion you reach from clues in the text plus what you already know. 'Her umbrella dripped on the floor' lets you infer that it was raining.
A deduction follows strictly from facts: if 'All of Class 8B went on the trip' and 'Neha is in 8B' are true, then 'Neha went on the trip' must be true.
Separate a fact (can be checked), an inference (a sensible conclusion from clues) and a guess (no clue supports it).
Read closely: one small word like 'not', 'only', 'all' or 'some' can change the whole meaning.
Codes and hidden messages use patterns, such as the first letter of each line (an acrostic) or one chosen word from each sentence.

example.q: Think it through: Find the hidden place in this note by reading the first letter of each line: 'Look under the mat / In the blue box / Behind the clock / Raju hid it / And then ran / Right back home / Yes, go now!'

topics.title: Modals of deduction: must, might and can't

learn.hook: A detective never says 'I think maybe perhaps...'. She says 'It MUST be him!' or 'It CAN'T be her!' Modals show how sure we are.
points: Modals of deduction show how certain we are about something.
must = almost certain it is true: The ground is wet. It must have rained.
might / may / could = possible, but not sure: He might be at the library.
can't = almost certain it is NOT true: She can't be at home; I just saw her at school.

topics.title: Fantasy tales and the shape of a story

learn.hook: What would you paint if everything you painted came alive? A fantasy tale lets you imagine exactly that.
points: 'The Magic Brush of Dreams' is a fantasy tale about art, imagination and using a gift fairly.
Fantasy stories include things that cannot happen in real life: magic objects, magical powers, talking animals or imaginary worlds. Yet they often carry real lessons about good and bad choices.
Every story has a setting (where and when), characters (who), and a plot (what happens).
A plot usually moves through: exposition (introduction), conflict (the problem), rising action (things get harder), climax (the turning point), and resolution (how it ends).
The protagonist is the main character. The antagonist is the person or force that works against the protagonist.

example.q: Read this original tale: 'In a dry village of Bundelkhand, a boy named Kabir found an old paint pot. Whatever he painted for others came alive, but nothing he painted for himself ever moved. When the village well dried up, Kabir painted dark rain clouds across the sky, and rain poured down. A greedy trader demanded a painted mountain of gold, but Kabir refused and painted a garden for the children instead.' Think it through: name the conflict and one fantasy element.
steps: The problem in the village is that the well has dried up; a second conflict is the greedy trader's demand.
A fantasy element is something impossible in real life: paintings that come alive.
The resolution: Kabir uses his gift for others, not for greed.
example.answer: Conflict: the dried-up well (and the greedy trader). Fantasy element: paintings that come to life.

learn.reallife: Animated films, comics and many grandparents' bedtime stories use fantasy to make us think about real values like honesty and sharing.

topics.title: Art and justice: values, word families and Indian art

learn.hook: A brush can make a picture. Can it also make things fair? Let's explore the words of justice.
points: Justice means fairness: giving people what they rightly deserve. In stories, justice is done when the honest are helped and the greedy are stopped.
Word family: just (adjective) → justice (noun) → justly (adverb); unjust and injustice are the opposites.

Negative prefixes: un- (unfair, unkind), dis- (dishonest, disagree), in- (inactive, incorrect, injustice). im- is used before p, m or b (impossible, immature, imbalance), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular, irresponsible).
Indian folk and traditional art: Madhubani (Bihar), Warli (Maharashtra), Pattachitra (Odisha), Gond (Madhya Pradesh), Tanjore painting (Tamil Nadu), Phad (Rajasthan).
Art can speak for justice: artists paint, sing and write to show unfairness and to imagine a better world.

example.q: Think it through: Add the correct prefix to make the opposite of each word: legal, possible, responsible, honest.
steps: 'legal' starts with l, so use il-: illegal.
'possible' starts with p, so use im-: impossible.
'responsible' starts with r, so use ir-: irresponsible.
'honest' takes dis-: dishonest.
example.answer: illegal, impossible, irresponsible, dishonest

learn.reallife: Warli wall paintings show village life with simple shapes, and Madhubani art is painted on walls, paper and cloth. Both can be seen at state handicraft melas.

topics.title: Describing art: degrees of comparison

learn.hook: Kabir's first painting was bright, his second was brighter, and his last was the brightest of all. Comparing is a painter's best tool!
points: Adjectives have three degrees: positive (bright), comparative (brighter, for two), superlative (brightest, for three or more). Use 'than' after a comparative and 'the' before a superlative.
Short adjectives add -er/-est: tall, taller, tallest. Double the last consonant after a single short vowel: big, bigger, biggest. Change -y to -i: pretty, prettier, prettiest.
Long adjectives use more/most: colourful, more colourful, most colourful.
Irregular forms: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.
Equality uses as...as: 'This Warli painting is as detailed as that one.' Not as/so...as shows a difference.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in the blanks: 'Of all the paintings in the mela, Kabir's was the ___ (good). It was ___ (colourful) than the trader's poster.'
steps: 'Of all' compares more than two, so use the superlative of good: best.
'than' compares two things, so use the comparative.
'Colourful' is long, so use 'more': more colourful.
example.answer: the best; more colourful

learn.reallife: Art competitions, cricket commentary and shopping all need comparisons: the best painting, a faster bowler, a cheaper kurta.

topics.title: Natural wonders of India

learn.hook: Bridges that grow, a lake with floating islands and a desert of white salt. These are not fairy tales; they are in India!
points: The lesson 'Spectacular Wonders' takes readers on a journey through amazing natural places and shows how to describe them vividly.
Living root bridges of Meghalaya are grown, not built: Khasi and Jaintia communities guide the roots of rubber fig trees across streams until they form strong bridges.
Loktak Lake in Manipur has floating masses of plants and soil called phumdis. On it lies Keibul Lamjao, the only floating national park in the world and the home of the sangai deer.
Lonar Lake in Maharashtra lies in a crater formed when a meteorite struck the Earth. The Great Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a vast white salt desert.

The Valley of Flowers in Uttarakhand blooms with wildflowers in the monsoon months; the Sundarbans in West Bengal is a mangrove forest, home to the Royal Bengal tiger; the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat in Madhya Pradesh line the Narmada river.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'At Bhedaghat, the Narmada slips between cliffs of white marble that rise like the walls of a giant's palace. When the moon shines, the rocks glow silver and the water whispers below.' Think it through: name the wonder, its river, and one comparison the writer uses.
steps: The place named is Bhedaghat, famous for its Marble Rocks.
The river named is the Narmada.
The comparison: cliffs 'rise like the walls of a giant's palace' (a simile using 'like').
'The water whispers' is personification too.
example.answer: The Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat on the Narmada; the cliffs are compared to the walls of a giant's palace.

learn.reallife: Many of these places are protected as national parks or World Heritage Sites. When we visit, we keep them clean and follow the rules so they stay wonderful.

topics.title: Prepositions of place and direction

learn.hook: Does a boat sail across the lake, through the lake or along the lake? One little word changes the whole picture!
points: Prepositions show the position or movement of something in relation to something else.

across = from one side to the other of a surface (across the river); through = from one end to the other inside something (through the tunnel, through the forest); along = following the length of something (along the beach).
in = inside (in the box); into = movement to the inside (jumped into the lake). on = resting on a surface; onto = movement to a surface.
between = with two things on either side; among = surrounded by many (among the trees).
beside = next to (sat beside the lake); besides = in addition to (Besides tigers, the Sundarbans has crocodiles).

example.q: Think it through: Choose the right prepositions: 'The train went ___ (through/across) a long tunnel and then ran ___ (along/among) the river for an hour.'
steps: A tunnel is something you go inside from one end to the other: through.

'Among' needs many things around you, not one river.
example.answer: through; along

topics.title: Ruskin Bond and his world of hills

learn.hook: Imagine a writer who looks out of his window at the mountains every morning and turns what he sees into stories. Meet Ruskin Bond!
points: 'The Cherry Tree' is a story by Ruskin Bond about a boy who plants a cherry seed and patiently watches it grow through the seasons and the years.
Ruskin Bond is an Indian author, born on 19 May 1934 in Kasauli, Himachal Pradesh. He has lived for many years in Landour, Mussoorie, in Uttarakhand.
He writes about the hills, trees, birds, small-town life and children, in simple, warm language. His first novel, 'The Room on the Roof', was written when he was a teenager.
His well-known works include 'The Blue Umbrella', the Rusty stories, and 'Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra', which won the Sahitya Akademi Award. He has received the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan.
His stories often show that small, everyday things, like a seed or a bird, hold great joy if we notice them.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'Tara pressed an apricot stone into the soil behind her house in Almora. For weeks nothing happened. She almost forgot it. Then one rainy morning she spotted two tiny green leaves pushing up through the earth, and she laughed out loud.' Think it through: what does Tara's laugh tell us, and what is the theme?
steps: For weeks nothing happened, so Tara had to wait.
When the leaves appeared, she laughed out loud: she was delighted.
The joy came after a long wait.
So the theme is that patience is rewarded with the joy of growth.
example.answer: Her laugh shows delight; the theme is that patience brings the joy of seeing something grow.

topics.title: Patience and growth: words of a growing tree

learn.hook: A tree does not grow when you shout at it. It grows a little every day while you wait. What words describe that journey?
points: A tree's life: a seed germinates (sprouts), becomes a seedling, then a sapling (a young tree), then a grown tree that flowers and bears fruit.
Growth words: bud (an unopened flower or leaf), blossom (flowers of a fruit tree), bloom (to flower), wither (to dry up and shrink), prune (to cut off extra branches).
Patience is the ability to wait calmly. Patient (adjective) → patience (noun) → patiently (adverb). The opposite is impatient/impatience.
Words related to patience: perseverance (keeping on trying), endurance (bearing difficulty). Proverb: 'Rome was not built in a day.'
Growth stories teach that care, time and hope together make things grow, whether it is a tree or a skill.

example.q: Think it through: Put the life of a fruit tree in order: sapling, seed, fruit, seedling, flowers.

The flowers turn into fruit.
example.answer: seed → seedling → sapling → flowers → fruit

topics.title: Time and growth: present perfect with since and for

learn.hook: 'The tree grew' is finished. 'The tree has grown' connects the past to now. One small helping verb, a big difference!
points: The present perfect tense = has/have + past participle: The tree has grown taller. We have planted ten saplings.
Use it for actions in the past whose result matters now, or for actions that began in the past and continue until now.
Use 'for' with a period of time (for three years, for two weeks) and 'since' with a point in time (since 2022, since Monday, since morning).
Do not use the present perfect with a finished past time like 'yesterday' or 'last year'. Say 'I planted it last year', not 'I have planted it last year'.
Present perfect continuous (has/have been + verb-ing) stresses that an action is still going on: It has been raining since morning.

example.q: Think it through: Fill in with 'since' or 'for': 'Rohan has watered the cherry tree every day ___ June. He has cared for it ___ four months.'

topics.title: A harvest poem: praise, personification and festivals

learn.hook: When fields turn gold, villages across India sing, dance and say thank you. A harvest poem joins that song.
points: 'Harvest Hymn' is a poem that celebrates the harvest and gives thanks to nature and to farmers' hard work.
A hymn is a song of praise. A harvest hymn praises the earth, rain and sun that help crops grow, and the people who grow them.
Personification gives human actions to non-human things: 'The golden fields bow low to greet the sun.' Fields cannot really bow, but the image shows heavy, ripe crops bending.
India celebrates harvest festivals in many regions: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Lohri and Baisakhi in Punjab, Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala, and Makar Sankranti in many states.

topics.title: Farmers and nature: crops, seasons and farm words

learn.hook: Rice loves the monsoon and wheat loves the winter. A farmer reads the seasons like a book!
points: Kharif crops are sown at the start of the monsoon (around June-July) and harvested around September-October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra.
Rabi crops are sown in winter (around October-November) and harvested in spring (around March-April): wheat, gram, mustard, barley, peas.

Farm work follows an order: ploughing (loosening the soil), sowing (planting seeds), irrigation (watering), weeding (removing unwanted plants), harvesting (cutting the crop), threshing (separating grain from stalks).
Collective nouns for farm and nature: a herd of cattle, a flock of birds, a swarm of locusts, a sheaf of wheat, a bunch of bananas.
Farmers depend on nature (rain, sunlight, healthy soil), so they care for it by saving water and keeping soil fertile.

example.q: Think it through: Ramesh sows seeds in June when the rains start, and harvests in October. Is his crop kharif or rabi, and which crop could it be: wheat or rice?
steps: Sown with the monsoon in June and harvested in October: that is the kharif season.
Rice is a kharif crop; wheat is a rabi crop.
So the crop is kharif, most likely rice.
example.answer: Kharif; rice
