topics.title: Rain and farming: the monsoon story

learn.hook: In June, millions of eyes across India look up at the sky together. They are all waiting for one guest: the monsoon!
points: 'Waiting for the Rain' is about how farming families wait for the rains, and how hope keeps them going.
The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June and then spreads across India. June to September is the main monsoon season and brings most of India's yearly rainfall.
Kharif crops like rice depend on monsoon rain. If the rain is late or too little, there may be a drought (a long period with too little rain); too much rain can cause floods.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecasts the weather. Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge, in millimetres.
Rain words: drizzle (light rain), downpour (very heavy rain), parched (very dry), humid (damp, sticky air), petrichor (the earthy smell when rain falls on dry ground).

example.q: Read this original passage: 'Every evening, Baba stood at the edge of the cracked field and studied the sky. The seeds waited in their sacks. One night, a cool wind rattled the tin roof, and the smell of wet earth drifted in. Baba smiled for the first time in weeks.' Think it through: why did Baba smile?
steps: The field was cracked, so it was very dry and the family needed rain.
The seeds were waiting in sacks: sowing needs rain.
A cool wind and the smell of wet earth are signs that rain has come or is coming.
So Baba smiled because the rain he was hoping for had arrived.
example.answer: He smiled because the cool wind and the smell of wet earth showed that the rain was finally coming, so he could sow his seeds.

topics.title: Hope: feeling words, suffixes and idioms

learn.hook: Even when the sky stays empty, a farmer keeps a sack of seeds ready. That is hope, and English has many ways to say it!
points: Hope is a feeling that something good will happen. Synonyms: optimism, expectation, faith. Antonyms: despair, hopelessness.
Suffixes change word meaning: -ful means 'full of' (hopeful, thankful, careful) and -less means 'without' (hopeless, careless, fearless, restless).
Word family: hope (noun/verb), hopeful (adjective), hopefully (adverb), hopeless (adjective), hopelessness (noun).

Idioms of hope: 'every cloud has a silver lining' (something good comes from bad times), 'light at the end of the tunnel' (a sign that a hard time is ending), 'keep your fingers crossed' (hope for luck), 'hope against hope' (keep hoping when chances are small).
Writers show hope through images of light, dawn, green shoots and clouds gathering.

example.q: Think it through: Read this original passage: 'Three weeks passed without rain. Many neighbours sold their bullocks. But Amma still cleaned the seed sacks every morning and said, "The clouds will come."' Which word best describes Amma: hopeful or hopeless?

She said, 'The clouds will come.' She believed good things would happen.
So she was hopeful, not hopeless.

topics.title: Talking about the future: will, going to, hope and wish

learn.hook: 'It will rain', 'It's going to rain', 'I hope it rains', 'I wish it would rain.' Four ways to talk about tomorrow!
points: 'Will' + base verb is used for predictions, promises and quick decisions: I think it will rain tomorrow. I'll help you carry the sacks.
'Be going to' + base verb is used for plans already made and for predictions based on what we can see now: We are going to sow rice next week. Look at those black clouds! It is going to rain.
The present continuous can show fixed future arrangements: We are leaving for the village on Saturday.
'Hope' is used for things that are possible: I hope it rains tomorrow. I hope you will come.
'Wish' is used for things that are unlikely or impossible now, often with a past form: I wish I could fly. I wish it were not so hot.

example.q: Think it through: Choose 'will' or 'going to': (a) 'Look at that sky! It ___ rain.' (b) 'Don't worry, I ___ water your plants while you are away.'

topics.title: Arthur C. Clarke and life on a space station

learn.hook: Can a tiny bird be useful hundreds of kilometres above the Earth? A famous science fiction writer thought so!
points: 'Feathered Friend' is a science fiction story by Arthur C. Clarke in which a small pet bird on a space station turns out to matter far more than anyone expected.

Arthur C. Clarke (1917-2008) was a British writer of science fiction who lived in Sri Lanka from 1956 until his death. In 1945 he wrote about using satellites in space to send signals around the world.
In the past, miners took canaries into coal mines. These birds react to dangerous gases like carbon monoxide sooner than people do, so a canary in trouble warned miners to get out.
On a space station, astronauts float because they are in free fall around the Earth (often called weightlessness or microgravity). Air, water and food must be carried up or recycled.
The International Space Station orbits about 400 km above the Earth and goes around it roughly every 90 minutes.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'On Moon Base Chandra, Ravi grew tomatoes under bright lamps. One morning every plant was drooping, though he had watered them the night before. He checked the water recycler and found it had stopped working.' Think it through: how did the plants help Ravi?
steps: Ravi had watered the plants, so drooping was unexpected.
The drooping was a warning sign that something was wrong.

So the plants acted like an early warning system.
example.answer: The drooping plants warned Ravi that the water recycler had failed, so he could find and fix the problem.

topics.title: Science fiction: imagining tomorrow with science

learn.hook: A robot that cooks dosa, a bus to Mars, a phone that translates birdsong. If it uses science to imagine the future, it's science fiction!
points: Science fiction (sci-fi) is imaginative writing based on science and technology. It asks 'What if...?' about the future, space, inventions or other worlds.
Sci-fi is different from fantasy: fantasy uses magic, while sci-fi tries to explain things through science, even when the science is imagined.
Common features: future or space settings, new inventions, scientists or astronauts as characters, and problems solved by reasoning.
Some sci-fi ideas later came true, such as communication satellites, video calls and robots.

India has its own sci-fi tradition, including Satyajit Ray's stories about the inventor Professor Shonku. India's real space journey includes Rakesh Sharma, the first Indian in space (1984), and Chandrayaan-3, which landed near the Moon's south pole on 23 August 2023.

example.q: Think it through: Is this science fiction or fantasy? 'In 2090, Asha boarded a solar-powered shuttle to a farm on Mars, where robots grew wheat inside glass domes.'
steps: Look at the setting: the future (2090) and Mars.
Look at the technology: a solar-powered shuttle, robots, glass domes.
Is there any magic? No, everything is explained by technology.
So it is science fiction.
example.answer: Science fiction

learn.reallife: Space missions by ISRO, like Chandrayaan and the Gaganyaan human spaceflight programme, show how yesterday's sci-fi dreams become today's science.

points: Many science words are built from roots and prefixes that come from Greek or Latin.

scope = look at (telescope, microscope); graph = write or draw (autograph, photograph); phone = sound (telephone, microphone); naut = sailor (astronaut).

topics.title: A poem on observing closely: imagery and looking words

learn.hook: Hold a magnifying glass over an ordinary leaf, and suddenly it looks like a map of rivers! Close looking turns the ordinary into the amazing.
points: 'Magnifying Glass' is a poem about looking closely at small things and discovering wonder in them.
A magnifying glass is a convex lens (thicker in the middle) that makes things look bigger than they are.
Imagery means word pictures that appeal to the senses. Poets use imagery and metaphors to show what close looking reveals: 'a beetle's back becomes a shining shield'.

Looking words have different shades of meaning: observe and examine (look carefully), peer (look closely, as if it is hard to see), inspect (check for details or faults), glance and glimpse (look quickly or briefly).
Close observation is the first step of science and of good writing: notice details, colours, shapes, patterns and changes.

example.q: Read this original poem: 'Through my glass a beetle's back / Becomes a shining shield of black; / A leaf turns into a map of streams, / A drop of dew holds rainbow gleams.' Think it through: what does the leaf become, and why is that a good image?
steps: The poem says the leaf 'turns into a map of streams'.
Under a magnifying glass, the veins of a leaf look like rivers branching on a map.
This is a metaphor: it compares the leaf directly to a map.
It helps us see the leaf's tiny veins in a new way.

topics.title: Curiosity: asking good questions and question tags

learn.hook: Why is the sky blue? How do ants find sugar? Every great discovery begins with a curious question!
points: Curiosity means a strong wish to know or learn. Curious (adjective) → curiosity (noun). Note the spelling: curiosity, not 'curiousity'.
Wh-questions ask for information: what, where, when, why, who, which, whose, how. 'Why do leaves change colour?'
Yes/no questions begin with a helping verb: Is, Are, Do, Does, Did, Can, Have. 'Does the lens make things bigger?'
In questions, the helping verb comes before the subject: 'Where does the beetle live?' (not 'Where the beetle lives?').

A question tag is a short question at the end of a sentence. A positive statement takes a negative tag and a negative statement takes a positive tag: 'It's a lens, isn't it?' 'You don't like spiders, do you?'

chapters.title: Bibha Chowdhuri: The Beam of Light that Lit the Path for Women in Indian Science

topics.title: Bibha Chowdhuri: the physicist who studied cosmic rays

learn.hook: Somewhere in the night sky, there is a star named after an Indian woman scientist. Who was she?
points: The lesson tells the life story of Bibha Chowdhuri, an Indian physicist whose work lit the way for women in Indian science.
Bibha Chowdhuri was born in 1913 in Calcutta (now Kolkata). She studied physics at the University of Calcutta at a time when very few women studied science.

At the Bose Institute in Kolkata, she worked with the physicist D. M. Bose. They used photographic plates to detect tiny particles produced by cosmic rays, which are high-energy particles that reach the Earth from outer space.

She earned her PhD at the University of Manchester in England, working in the laboratory of Patrick Blackett, who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1948. Back in India she worked at research centres such as the Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and the Physical Research Laboratory.
In 2019, the International Astronomical Union named a star 'Bibha' in her honour.

example.q: Read this original passage: 'In the 1930s, most girls in Bengal were not encouraged to study science. Bibha chose physics anyway, sat in classrooms full of young men, and went on to study particles that come from far beyond the Earth.' Think it through: which two qualities does this passage show?
steps: Girls were not encouraged, yet she chose physics: that shows courage and determination.
She went on to study particles from space: that shows curiosity and love of science.
The word 'anyway' shows that she did not let others' expectations stop her.
example.answer: Determination (she chose physics anyway) and curiosity (she studied particles from beyond the Earth).

learn.reallife: When you see a girl topping a science olympiad or building a robot at a school fair, she is walking on a path that pioneers like Bibha Chowdhuri helped to open.

topics.title: Women in Indian science: pioneers and the words to describe them

learn.hook: A botanist who improved sugarcane, a 'weather woman', a 'missile woman' and an astronaut! India's women scientists have done it all.
points: Janaki Ammal was a botanist who worked on breeding better sugarcane. Asima Chatterjee was a chemist who studied medicines made from plants.
Anna Mani was a physicist and meteorologist who made instruments for measuring the weather. Kamala Sohonie was a biochemist who studied the nutrition in foods.

Kalpana Chawla, born in Karnal, Haryana, became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space, in 1997. Tessy Thomas, a scientist at DRDO, is known as the 'Missile Woman of India' for her work on the Agni missiles.
A pioneer is one of the first people to do something and so opens the way for others. Many of these women were pioneers.
Words to describe them: determined, brilliant, dedicated, inspiring, persistent. Nouns: determination, dedication, inspiration, achievement.

topics.title: Writing about a life: relative pronouns

learn.hook: 'Bibha was a physicist. She studied cosmic rays.' Two short sentences, or one smooth one? Relative pronouns do the joining!
points: A relative pronoun joins two ideas and refers back to a noun: who, which, whose, whom, that. 'Where' and 'when' can join clauses about places and times.
who = for people: Bibha was a physicist who studied cosmic rays.
which = for things and animals: The star which was named after her is far beyond our Solar System. That can be used for people or things in many sentences.
whose = shows possession: D. M. Bose was the scientist whose laboratory she worked in.
where = for places; when = for times: Kolkata is the city where she was born. 1913 was the year when she was born.

example.q: Think it through: Join these sentences with a relative pronoun: 'Kalpana Chawla was an astronaut. Her first space flight was in 1997.'
steps: The second sentence talks about something that belongs to Kalpana Chawla: 'her first space flight'.
Possession is shown with 'whose'.
Replace 'Her' with 'whose' and join.
example.answer: Kalpana Chawla was an astronaut whose first space flight was in 1997.

learn.reallife: Biographies, encyclopedias and school project reports use relative pronouns to pack facts smoothly: 'Kolkata, where she was born, ...'
